claim: Familial dysautonomia (FD) is a sensory and autonomic neuropathy caused by mutations in elongator complex protein 1 (ELP1).
source: Familial dysautonomia (FD) is a sensory and autonomic neuropathy caused by mutations in elongator complex protein 1 (ELP1).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about FD supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: FD patients have small trigeminal nerves and impaired facial pain and temperature perception.
source: FD patients have small trigeminal nerves and impaired facial pain and temperature perception.
evidence: Cited clinical observations about FD patients.

claim: The trigeminal ganglion is composed of both neural crest- and placode-derived cells.
source: These signals are relayed by nociceptive neurons in the trigeminal ganglion, a structure that is composed of both neural crest- and placode-derived cells.
evidence: Established developmental biology knowledge about trigeminal ganglion composition.

claim: Mice lacking Elp1 in neural crest derivatives ('Elp1 CKO') are born with small trigeminal ganglia.
source: Mice lacking Elp1 in neural crest derivatives ('Elp1 CKO') are born with small trigeminal ganglia, suggesting Elp1 is important for trigeminal ganglion development, yet the function of Elp1 in this context is unknown.
evidence: Cited observation from previous studies.

claim: Elp1 is expressed in both neural crest- and placode-derived neurons in the trigeminal ganglion.
source: We demonstrate that Elp1, expressed in both neural crest- and placode-derived neurons, is not required for initial trigeminal ganglion formation.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data in the manuscript.

claim: Elp1 is not required for initial trigeminal ganglion formation.
source: We demonstrate that Elp1, expressed in both neural crest- and placode-derived neurons, is not required for initial trigeminal ganglion formation.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing Control and Elp1 CKO embryos at E10.5.

claim: Elp1 CKO trigeminal neurons exhibit abnormal axon outgrowth and deficient target innervation.
source: However, Elp1 CKO trigeminal neurons exhibit abnormal axon outgrowth and deficient target innervation.
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry and imaging data.

claim: Developing nociceptors expressing the receptor TrkA undergo early apoptosis in Elp1 CKO.
source: Developing nociceptors expressing the receptor TrkA undergo early apoptosis in Elp1 CKO, while TrkB- and TrkC-expressing neurons are spared, indicating Elp1 supports the target innervation and survival of trigeminal nociceptors.
evidence: Demonstrated by TUNEL assays and cell counting data.

claim: TrkB- and TrkC-expressing neurons are spared in Elp1 CKO.
source: Developing nociceptors expressing the receptor TrkA undergo early apoptosis in Elp1 CKO, while TrkB- and TrkC-expressing neurons are spared, indicating Elp1 supports the target innervation and survival of trigeminal nociceptors.
evidence: Demonstrated by cell counting and immunohistochemistry data.

claim: Elp1 supports the target innervation and survival of trigeminal nociceptors.
source: Developing nociceptors expressing the receptor TrkA undergo early apoptosis in Elp1 CKO, while TrkB- and TrkC-expressing neurons are spared, indicating Elp1 supports the target innervation and survival of trigeminal nociceptors.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TrkA neurons undergo apoptosis and have innervation defects in Elp1 CKO.

claim: Most TrkA neurons in the trigeminal ganglion are neural crest-derived.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that specific TrkA deficits in the Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglion reflect the neural crest lineage of most TrkA neurons versus the placodal lineage of most TrkB and TrkC neurons.
evidence: Demonstrated by lineage tracing experiments using Wnt1-Cre; ROSAmT/mG reporter mice.

claim: Most TrkB and TrkC neurons in the trigeminal ganglion are placode-derived.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that specific TrkA deficits in the Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglion reflect the neural crest lineage of most TrkA neurons versus the placodal lineage of most TrkB and TrkC neurons.
evidence: Demonstrated by lineage tracing experiments using Wnt1-Cre; ROSAmT/mG reporter mice.

claim: The FD mutation causes mis-splicing and skipping of exon 20 in a tissue-specific manner.
source: The most prevalent form is HSAN type III, or familial dysautonomia (FD), which is almost exclusively caused by a mutation in intron 20 of the elongator complex protein 1 (ELP1, formerly IKBKAP) gene (Anderson et al., 2001; Slaugenhaupt et al., 2001). This mutation causes mis-splicing and skipping of exon 20 in a tissue-specific manner, consequently reducing ELP1 protein in neurons (Slaugenhaupt et al., 2001; Hims et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from previous studies on the molecular basis of FD.

claim: The FD mutation reduces ELP1 protein in neurons.
source: This mutation causes mis-splicing and skipping of exon 20 in a tissue-specific manner, consequently reducing ELP1 protein in neurons (Slaugenhaupt et al., 2001; Hims et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from previous studies on the molecular basis of FD.

claim: Elp1 is a requisite scaffolding protein of the six-subunit elongator complex.
source: Elp1 is a requisite scaffolding protein of the six-subunit elongator complex that regulates translation by modifying particular tRNAs (Huang et al., 2005; Huang et al., 2008; Karlsborn et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2015; Esberg et al., 2006).
evidence: Cited from previous studies on elongator complex function.

claim: The elongator complex regulates translation by modifying particular tRNAs.
source: Elp1 is a requisite scaffolding protein of the six-subunit elongator complex that regulates translation by modifying particular tRNAs (Huang et al., 2005; Huang et al., 2008; Karlsborn et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2015; Esberg et al., 2006).
evidence: Cited from previous studies on elongator complex function.

claim: Deletion of elongator subunits alters tRNA modifications and protein expression in several systems.
source: Deletion of elongator subunits has been shown to alter tRNA modifications and protein expression in several systems (Cameron et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2009b; Esberg et al., 2006; Goffena et al., 2018; Karlsborn et al., 2014; Kojic et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from multiple previous studies.

claim: FD clinical phenotypes include impaired pain and temperature sensation, feeding and swallowing difficulties, blood pressure instability, tachycardia, optic neuropathy, and gastrointestinal dysfunction.
source: Consequently, loss or reduction of Elp1 protein leads directly or indirectly to the clinical phenotypes seen in FD, which include impaired pain and temperature sensation, feeding and swallowing difficulties, blood pressure instability, tachycardia, optic neuropathy, and gastrointestinal dysfunction, among other symptoms.
evidence: Established clinical knowledge about FD symptoms.

claim: The majority of FD patients die by age 50.
source: The disease is fatal, with the majority of patients dying by age 50 (Gold-von Simson and Axelrod, 2006).
evidence: Cited clinical outcome data.

claim: FD phenotypes are caused by abnormal neurodevelopment and neurodegeneration across the lifespan.
source: Autopsy reports, patient studies, and animal models demonstrate FD phenotypes are caused by abnormal neurodevelopment, in addition to neurodegeneration across the lifespan of the affected individual (Pearson et al., 1978; Hunnicutt et al., 2012; George et al., 2013; Jackson et al., 2014; Li et al., 2020; Won et al., 2019; Lefcort et al., 2017; Dietrich and Dragatsis, 2016).
evidence: Cited from multiple previous studies.

claim: The peripheral nervous system is composed of sensory and autonomic neurons that are mostly derived from neural crest cells and some cranial sensory neurons that arise from ectodermal placodes.
source: FD severely impacts the peripheral nervous system, composed of sensory and autonomic neurons that are mostly derived from neural crest cells and some cranial sensory neurons that arise from ectodermal placodes (Méndez-Maldonado et al., 2020; Steventon et al., 2014; Kameneva and Adameyko, 2019).
evidence: Established developmental biology knowledge.

claim: Mice null for Elp1 are embryonic lethal.
source: Since mice null for Elp1 are embryonic lethal (Chen et al., 2009a; Dietrich et al., 2011), FD has been modeled in mice using conditional knockout of Elp1 in neural crest cells (Elp1fl/fl; Wnt1-Cre+, abbreviated 'Elp1 CKO'), which recapitulates several aspects of the human disease, including significant loss of sensory and autonomic neurons (George et al., 2013; Jackson et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from previous studies.

claim: The Elp1 CKO mouse model recapitulates several aspects of human FD, including significant loss of sensory and autonomic neurons.
source: Since mice null for Elp1 are embryonic lethal (Chen et al., 2009a; Dietrich et al., 2011), FD has been modeled in mice using conditional knockout of Elp1 in neural crest cells (Elp1fl/fl; Wnt1-Cre+, abbreviated 'Elp1 CKO'), which recapitulates several aspects of the human disease, including significant loss of sensory and autonomic neurons (George et al., 2013; Jackson et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from previous studies.

claim: FD patients experience impaired sensation of facial pain and temperature, neurogenic dysphagia, absent corneal reflexes, and reduced basal lacrimation.
source: However, FD patients also experience cranial sensory deficits such as impaired sensation of facial pain and temperature, neurogenic dysphagia, absent corneal reflexes, and reduced basal lacrimation (Mendoza-Santiesteban et al., 2017; Palma et al., 2014; Barlow, 2009; Geltzer et al., 1964; Gutiérrez et al., 2015; Palma et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited clinical observations.

claim: The trigeminal nerve is the largest of the cranial nerves.
source: These functions rely on input from the trigeminal nerve, the largest of the cranial nerves, which contains axons of sensory neurons that reside in the trigeminal ganglion.
evidence: Established anatomical knowledge.

claim: FD patients have smaller trigeminal nerves compared to healthy, age-matched individuals.
source: A quantitative MRI study revealed FD patients have smaller trigeminal nerves compared to healthy, age-matched individuals, but there are no indications of progressive trigeminal nerve degeneration (Won et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from a quantitative MRI study.

claim: There are no indications of progressive trigeminal nerve degeneration in FD patients.
source: A quantitative MRI study revealed FD patients have smaller trigeminal nerves compared to healthy, age-matched individuals, but there are no indications of progressive trigeminal nerve degeneration (Won et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from a quantitative MRI study.

claim: Trigeminal ganglia of Elp1 CKO mice are reduced in size at birth compared to Controls.
source: Moreover, trigeminal ganglia of Elp1 CKO mice are reduced in size at birth compared to Controls (Jackson et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from a previous study.

claim: Peripheral neurons in the trunk are exclusively neural crest-derived.
source: While peripheral neurons in the trunk are exclusively neural crest-derived, cranial sensory neurons arise from two progenitor populations, neural crest cells and ectodermal placodes, which typically contribute neurons to spatially distinct regions of the cranial ganglia (York et al., 2020; Moody and LaMantia, 2015; Park and Saint-Jeannet, 2010; Steventon et al., 2014).
evidence: Established developmental biology knowledge.

claim: Cranial sensory neurons arise from two progenitor populations: neural crest cells and ectodermal placodes.
source: While peripheral neurons in the trunk are exclusively neural crest-derived, cranial sensory neurons arise from two progenitor populations, neural crest cells and ectodermal placodes, which typically contribute neurons to spatially distinct regions of the cranial ganglia (York et al., 2020; Moody and LaMantia, 2015; Park and Saint-Jeannet, 2010; Steventon et al., 2014).
evidence: Established developmental biology knowledge.

claim: The trigeminal ganglion contains intermixed neural crest- and placode-derived neurons that rely on one another for proper migration, coalescence, and function during development.
source: The trigeminal ganglion is unique in that it contains intermixed neural crest- and placode-derived neurons that rely on one another for proper migration, coalescence, and function during development (Blentic et al., 2011; D'Amico-Martel, 1982; D'Amico-Martel and Noden, 1983; Freter et al., 2013; Hamburger, 1961; Saint-Jeannet and Moody, 2014; Shiau et al., 2008; Steventon et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from multiple previous studies.

claim: Trigeminal ganglion neuron subtypes are discernable by mutually exclusive expression of tropomyosin receptor kinase (Trk) receptors: TrkA, TrkB, or TrkC.
source: Shortly after differentiation, trigeminal ganglion neuron subtypes are discernable by mutually exclusive expression of tropomyosin receptor kinase (Trk) receptors, TrkA, TrkB, or TrkC, which are required for target innervation and long-term survival (Huang et al., 1999a; Wilkinson et al., 1996; Scott-Solomon and Kuruvilla, 2018; Davies, 1997; Reichardt, 2006; Huang et al., 1999b).
evidence: Cited from previous studies.

claim: Trk receptors are required for target innervation and long-term survival of trigeminal ganglion neurons.
source: Shortly after differentiation, trigeminal ganglion neuron subtypes are discernable by mutually exclusive expression of tropomyosin receptor kinase (Trk) receptors, TrkA, TrkB, or TrkC, which are required for target innervation and long-term survival (Huang et al., 1999a; Wilkinson et al., 1996; Scott-Solomon and Kuruvilla, 2018; Davies, 1997; Reichardt, 2006; Huang et al., 1999b).
evidence: Cited from previous studies.

claim: Small-diameter TrkA neurons are typically associated with pain and temperature perception.
source: Importantly, Trk expression generally correlates with the ultimate sensory modality encoded by a particular neuron; for example, small-diameter TrkA neurons are typically associated with pain and temperature perception, while large-diameter TrkB and TrkC neurons are usually mechanoreceptors that sense touch, pressure, and vibrations (Mu et al., 1993; Genç et al., 2005; d'Amico-Martel and Noden, 1980; D'Amico-Martel and Noden, 1983; Davies and Lumsden, 1984).
evidence: Cited from previous studies.

claim: Large-diameter TrkB and TrkC neurons are usually mechanoreceptors that sense touch, pressure, and vibrations.
source: Importantly, Trk expression generally correlates with the ultimate sensory modality encoded by a particular neuron; for example, small-diameter TrkA neurons are typically associated with pain and temperature perception, while large-diameter TrkB and TrkC neurons are usually mechanoreceptors that sense touch, pressure, and vibrations (Mu et al., 1993; Genç et al., 2005; d'Amico-Martel and Noden, 1980; D'Amico-Martel and Noden, 1983; Davies and Lumsden, 1984).
evidence: Cited from previous studies.

claim: In dorsal root, epibranchial, and sympathetic ganglia, Elp1 is required for the generation and/or survival of TrkA and TrkB neurons, while TrkC neurons are spared during development.
source: In dorsal root, epibranchial (sensory), and sympathetic (autonomic) ganglia, Elp1 is required for the generation and/or survival of TrkA and TrkB neurons, while TrkC neurons are spared during development (George et al., 2013; Jackson et al., 2014; Tolman et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited from previous studies.

claim: Neuronal loss in dorsal root, epibranchial, and sympathetic ganglia has been attributed to decreased neurogenesis resulting from early differentiation and apoptosis of progenitors.
source: In these contexts, neuronal loss has been attributed to decreased neurogenesis resulting from early differentiation and apoptosis of progenitors (George et al., 2013; Goffena et al., 2018) and to severe target innervation defects and neuronal apoptosis due to insufficient neurotrophic support (Jackson et al., 2014; Li et al., 2020; Tolman et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited from previous studies.

claim: Neuronal loss in dorsal root, epibranchial, and sympathetic ganglia has been attributed to severe target innervation defects and neuronal apoptosis due to insufficient neurotrophic support.
source: In these contexts, neuronal loss has been attributed to decreased neurogenesis resulting from early differentiation and apoptosis of progenitors (George et al., 2013; Goffena et al., 2018) and to severe target innervation defects and neuronal apoptosis due to insufficient neurotrophic support (Jackson et al., 2014; Li et al., 2020; Tolman et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited from previous studies.

claim: Other less common forms of HSANs arise from germline mutations in the genes encoding either TrkA or its high-affinity ligand, nerve growth factor (NGF).
source: Notably, other less common forms of HSANs arise from germline mutations in the genes encoding either TrkA or its high-affinity ligand, nerve growth factor (NGF; Schwartzlow and Kazamel, 2019).
evidence: Cited from a review on HSANs.

claim: Evidence from animal models suggests Elp1 regulates TrkA signaling.
source: A growing body of evidence from animal models suggests Elp1 regulates TrkA signaling as well (Abashidze et al., 2014; Lefler et al., 2015; Naftelberg et al., 2016; Li et al., 2020), although the relationship between Elp1 and TrkA has not been investigated in the cranial ganglia.
evidence: Cited from previous animal model studies.

claim: The relationship between Elp1 and TrkA has not been investigated in the cranial ganglia.
source: A growing body of evidence from animal models suggests Elp1 regulates TrkA signaling as well (Abashidze et al., 2014; Lefler et al., 2015; Naftelberg et al., 2016; Li et al., 2020), although the relationship between Elp1 and TrkA has not been investigated in the cranial ganglia.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Elp1 protein is enriched in the cytoplasm of differentiated neurons in the trigeminal ganglion at E10.5.
source: Detection of Elp1 via immunohistochemistry revealed a similar expression pattern to that found in the Elp1LacZ reporter; however, Elp1 protein was more discretely expressed compared to β-galactosidase. At E10.5, Elp1 protein was abundant in the cytoplasm of differentiated neurons, which were identified by expression of the transcription factor Islet1 (Figure 1D–G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Elp1 is initially expressed in trigeminal placode-derived neurons at E10.5.
source: Since the majority of neurons in the trigeminal ganglion are placode-derived at this stage, while surrounding neural crest cells have yet to differentiate (Karpinski et al., 2016), it appears that Elp1 is initially expressed in trigeminal placode-derived neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Elp1 is expressed in differentiated neurons at E10.5, which are predominantly placode-derived at this stage.

claim: Condensed neural crest cells within the trigeminal ganglion at E10.5 express little to no Elp1 protein.
source: In contrast, condensed neural crest cells within the trigeminal ganglion, identified by expression of the surface receptor Neuropilin 2 or the transcription factor Pax3, and devoid of Islet1, expressed little to no Elp1 protein (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-D).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: At E11.5, Elp1 protein is observed in all differentiated neurons expressing β-tubulin III or Islet1, irrespective of their developmental origin.
source: At E11.5, when neural crest-derived neurons are also present in the trigeminal ganglion, Elp1 protein was observed in all differentiated neurons expressing β-tubulin III (Tubb3) or Islet1, irrespective of their developmental origin, with the highest signal detected in axons (Figure 1H–M and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-H).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The highest Elp1 signal at E11.5 is detected in axons.
source: At E11.5, when neural crest-derived neurons are also present in the trigeminal ganglion, Elp1 protein was observed in all differentiated neurons expressing β-tubulin III (Tubb3) or Islet1, irrespective of their developmental origin, with the highest signal detected in axons (Figure 1H–M and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-H).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: By E12.5, Elp1 protein is enriched in the neuronal cytoplasm, especially axons.
source: By E12.5, enrichment of Elp1 protein in the neuronal cytoplasm, especially axons, is still apparent, while Elp1 is absent or expressed at relatively low levels in neural crest-derived Sox10-positive glia (Figure 1N–P).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Elp1 is absent or expressed at relatively low levels in neural crest-derived Sox10-positive glia at E12.5.
source: By E12.5, enrichment of Elp1 protein in the neuronal cytoplasm, especially axons, is still apparent, while Elp1 is absent or expressed at relatively low levels in neural crest-derived Sox10-positive glia (Figure 1N–P).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: At E10.5, initial formation of the trigeminal ganglion appeared normal in Elp1 CKO compared to Controls.
source: When compared to littermate Controls at E10.5, initial formation of the trigeminal ganglion appeared normal in Elp1 CKO (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 2.

claim: There is no significant difference in the size of the trigeminal ganglion at E10.5 between Control and Elp1 CKO.
source: Gross anatomy was intact with no significant difference in the size of the trigeminal ganglion (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The ophthalmic, maxillary, and mandibular nerve branches are all present in both Control and Elp1 CKO at E10.5.
source: The ophthalmic, maxillary, and mandibular nerve branches were all present in both Control and Elp1 CKO (Figure 2B and C), with no significant changes in the length of the ophthalmic nerve (618.7 µm Control, n=3, versus 569.0 µm Elp1 CKO, n=3, p=0.0520, unpaired t-test, Holm-Sidak adjustment for multiple comparisons) nor the mandibular nerve (896.3 µm Control, n=3, versus 905.0 µm Elp1 CKO, n=3, p=0.832, unpaired t-test, Holm-Sidak adjustment for multiple comparisons).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 2.

claim: There are no significant changes in the length of the ophthalmic nerve at E10.5 between Control and Elp1 CKO.
source: The ophthalmic, maxillary, and mandibular nerve branches were all present in both Control and Elp1 CKO (Figure 2B and C), with no significant changes in the length of the ophthalmic nerve (618.7 µm Control, n=3, versus 569.0 µm Elp1 CKO, n=3, p=0.0520, unpaired t-test, Holm-Sidak adjustment for multiple comparisons) nor the mandibular nerve (896.3 µm Control, n=3, versus 905.0 µm Elp1 CKO, n=3, p=0.832, unpaired t-test, Holm-Sidak adjustment for multiple comparisons).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of nerve length.

claim: There are no significant changes in the length of the mandibular nerve at E10.5 between Control and Elp1 CKO.
source: The ophthalmic, maxillary, and mandibular nerve branches were all present in both Control and Elp1 CKO (Figure 2B and C), with no significant changes in the length of the ophthalmic nerve (618.7 µm Control, n=3, versus 569.0 µm Elp1 CKO, n=3, p=0.0520, unpaired t-test, Holm-Sidak adjustment for multiple comparisons) nor the mandibular nerve (896.3 µm Control, n=3, versus 905.0 µm Elp1 CKO, n=3, p=0.832, unpaired t-test, Holm-Sidak adjustment for multiple comparisons).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of nerve length.

claim: Placodal neurons and undifferentiated neural crest cells are present in similar ratios throughout the forming trigeminal ganglion at E10.5 in Control and Elp1 CKO.
source: Immunohistochemistry on E10.5 tissue sections revealed placodal neurons (Islet1-positive and Six1-positive nuclei) and undifferentiated neural crest cells (Sox10-positive nuclei) present in similar ratios throughout the forming trigeminal ganglion (Figure 2E–J).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 2.

claim: There is no change in the size or length of the exclusively placode-derived geniculate ganglion or chorda tympani nerve at E10.5 between Control and Elp1 CKO.
source: There was also no change in the size or length of the exclusively placode-derived geniculate ganglion (387 µm Control, n=3, versus 361 µm Elp1 CKO, n=3, p=0.4559, unpaired t-test, Holm-Sidak adjustment for multiple comparisons) or chorda tympani nerve (692 µm Control, n=3, versus 686.3 µm Elp1 CKO, n=3, p=0.7671, unpaired t-test, Holm-Sidak adjustment for multiple comparisons), whose neurons are not targeted by Wnt1-Cre for Elp1 deletion (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry and quantification.

claim: Elp1 is not required in neural crest cells for them to coalesce with placodal neurons as the trigeminal ganglion is initially forming.
source: Altogether, these data suggest Elp1 is not required in neural crest cells for them to coalesce with placodal neurons as the trigeminal ganglion is initially forming.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that trigeminal ganglion formation appears normal at E10.5 in Elp1 CKO.

claim: By E11.5, Control and Elp1 CKO display robust outgrowth of axons from the trigeminal ganglion.
source: By E11.5, Control and Elp1 CKO displayed robust outgrowth of axons from the trigeminal ganglion, which contains both neural crest- and placode-derived neurons at this stage (Figure 3B and E).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3.

claim: At E11.5, nerves in Elp1 CKO appeared less organized than in Controls.
source: Although the ophthalmic, maxillary, and mandibular nerves were present and distinct in Control and Elp1 CKO, nerves in the latter appeared less organized.
evidence: Observed from whole-mount immunohistochemistry images.

claim: In the maxillary nerve at E11.5, Elp1 CKO axons often strayed from established bundles into the surrounding mesenchyme or crossed to adjacent fascicles.
source: In the maxillary nerve, Elp1 CKO axons often strayed from established bundles into the surrounding mesenchyme or crossed to adjacent fascicles (Figure 3C and F).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3.

claim: Axons of the mandibular nerve in Elp1 CKO at E11.5 traveled away from the established nerve without direction, compared to the compact mandibular nerve observed in Controls.
source: Axons of the mandibular nerve in Elp1 CKO also traveled away from the established nerve without direction, compared to the compact mandibular nerve observed in Controls (Figure 3D and G).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3.

claim: The Elp1 CKO phenotype is highly penetrant, with disrupted axon trajectories noted to varying degrees in all Elp1 CKO embryos examined.
source: The Elp1 CKO phenotype is highly penetrant, and disrupted axon trajectories were noted to varying degrees in all Elp1 CKO embryos examined.
evidence: Observation across multiple Elp1 CKO embryos.

claim: The placode-derived chorda tympani nerve exhibited normal axon trajectories in both Control and Elp1 CKO embryos at E11.5.
source: In contrast, the placode-derived chorda tympani nerve exhibited normal axon trajectories in both Control and Elp1 CKO embryos at E11.5 (Figure 3B and E).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3.

claim: At E11.5, there is no significant difference in the size of the trigeminal ganglion between Control and Elp1 CKO.
source: At this stage, there was no significant difference in the size of the trigeminal ganglion or the width of the central nerve root, which contains axons projecting from the trigeminal ganglion into the hindbrain, in Control versus Elp1 CKO (Figure 3H and I).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 3.

claim: At E11.5, there is no significant difference in the width of the central nerve root between Control and Elp1 CKO.
source: At this stage, there was no significant difference in the size of the trigeminal ganglion or the width of the central nerve root, which contains axons projecting from the trigeminal ganglion into the hindbrain, in Control versus Elp1 CKO (Figure 3H and I).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 3.

claim: At E11.5, there are similar ratios of Sox10-positive cells and Six1-positive cells in Control and Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglia.
source: Additionally, there were similar ratios of Sox10-positive cells (Control = 47.1%, n=3, versus Elp1 CKO = 50.3%, n=3, of all DAPI-stained nuclei, p=0.6444, nested two-tailed t-test) and Six1-positive cells (Control = 69.7%, n=3, versus Elp1 CKO = 65.9%, n=3, of all DAPI-stained nuclei, p=0.4897, nested t-test) in Control and Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglia.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of immunohistochemistry data.

claim: By E12.5, trigeminal ganglion and nerve morphology were drastically altered in Elp1 CKO.
source: By E12.5, trigeminal ganglion and nerve morphology were drastically altered in Elp1 CKO, with nuanced changes in specific nerve branches (Figure 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 4.

claim: The size of the trigeminal ganglion at E12.5 trended smaller in Elp1 CKO but was not statistically significant.
source: The size of the trigeminal ganglion proper trended smaller but was not statistically significant (Figure 4B, E and H).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 4.

claim: The diameter of the nerve root at E12.5 was significantly smaller in Elp1 CKO compared to Control.
source: Interestingly, the diameter of the nerve root was significantly smaller in Elp1 CKO, indicating the loss of some centrally projecting axons between E11.5 and E12.5 (Figure 4B, E and I).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 4.

claim: The loss of centrally projecting axons occurs between E11.5 and E12.5 in Elp1 CKO.
source: Interestingly, the diameter of the nerve root was significantly smaller in Elp1 CKO, indicating the loss of some centrally projecting axons between E11.5 and E12.5 (Figure 4B, E and I).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that the central root diameter is normal at E11.5 but significantly smaller at E12.5.

claim: The branching complexity of the frontal nerve at E12.5 is decreased in Elp1 CKO compared to Control.
source: The developing frontal nerve (ophthalmic division) was present in both Control and Elp1 CKO; however, the branching complexity of the nerve was decreased in Elp1 CKO, as quantified by a modified Sholl analysis (Figure 4C, F, J, and K, Sholl, 1953).
evidence: Demonstrated by modified Sholl analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Stray frontal nerve axons are observed proximal to the ganglion in Elp1 CKO at E12.5.
source: Stray frontal nerve axons were also observed proximal to the ganglion (Figure 4F).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 4.

claim: The medial and lateral nasal nerves are absent in Elp1 CKO at E12.5.
source: While the ophthalmic nerve extended rostrally in both Control and Elp1 CKO, the medial and lateral nasal nerves that descend from this branch toward the nose were absent in Elp1 CKO (Figure 4D and G).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 4.

claim: The terminal extent of the infraorbital nerve at E12.5 is smaller in Elp1 CKO compared to Control.
source: The maxillary division was also impacted, such that the terminal extent of the infraorbital nerve, which innervates the whisker pad, was smaller in Elp1 CKO compared to Control (Figure 4D, G and L).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 4.

claim: Nerve defects caused by loss of Elp1 can differ within the same ganglion, based on neuronal identity and/or specific target region.
source: Together, these results provide a dynamic summary of the requirements for Elp1 in axonal pathfinding and target innervation in trigeminal ganglion sensory neurons. Importantly, our data suggest that nerve defects caused by loss of Elp1 can differ, even within the same ganglion, based on neuronal identity and/or specific target region.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that different nerve branches show distinct phenotypes in Elp1 CKO.

claim: TrkA expression at E13 is strong throughout the trigeminal ganglion and along all three major nerve divisions in Control embryos.
source: In Control embryos, TrkA expression was strong throughout the trigeminal ganglion and along all three major nerve divisions, detectable into the most distal branches of the frontal and infraorbital nerves (Figure 5A, B, E, and F, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5.

claim: TrkA immunoreactivity at E13 is drastically reduced in the central nerve root and in distal branches of the frontal nerve, the rostral ophthalmic nerve, and the infraorbital nerve in Elp1 CKO.
source: In Elp1 CKO, TrkA immunoreactivity was drastically reduced in the central nerve root (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,D) and in distal branches of the frontal nerve, the rostral ophthalmic nerve, and the infraorbital nerve (Figure 5C, D, G, and H), indicating effects on both central and peripheral trigeminal projections.
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5.

claim: TrkA immunofluorescence at E12.5 is significantly reduced in Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglia compared to Control.
source: Examination of E12.5 tissue sections through the maxillary lobe revealed significantly reduced TrkA immunofluorescence in Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglia compared to Control, with no change in TrkB or TrkC immunofluorescence (Figure 5I–L and Q and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-L).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 5.

claim: There is no change in TrkB or TrkC immunofluorescence at E12.5 in Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglia compared to Control.
source: Examination of E12.5 tissue sections through the maxillary lobe revealed significantly reduced TrkA immunofluorescence in Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglia compared to Control, with no change in TrkB or TrkC immunofluorescence (Figure 5I–L and Q and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-L).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 5.

claim: There are fewer TrkA-expressing nerve endings in the upper lip at E12.5 in Elp1 CKO compared to Control.
source: Sections through the upper lip, which is heavily innervated by the infraorbital nerve, demonstrated fewer TrkA-expressing nerve endings in Elp1 CKO compared to Control, while TrkC-expressing nerve endings were maintained (Figure 5M–P).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5.

claim: TrkC-expressing nerve endings in the upper lip are maintained at E12.5 in Elp1 CKO.
source: Sections through the upper lip, which is heavily innervated by the infraorbital nerve, demonstrated fewer TrkA-expressing nerve endings in Elp1 CKO compared to Control, while TrkC-expressing nerve endings were maintained (Figure 5M–P).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5.

claim: TrkA neurons are reduced by 23% in Elp1 CKO compared to Controls at E12.5.
source: While no differences were observed in the number of TrkB or TrkC neurons, TrkA neurons were reduced by 23% in Elp1 CKO compared to Controls (Figure 5R).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 5.

claim: There are no differences in the number of TrkB or TrkC neurons at E12.5 between Control and Elp1 CKO.
source: While no differences were observed in the number of TrkB or TrkC neurons, TrkA neurons were reduced by 23% in Elp1 CKO compared to Controls (Figure 5R).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 5.

claim: Early target innervation defects in Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglion neurons are associated with a specific loss of TrkA-expressing neurons in the ganglion and nerves.
source: Therefore, early target innervation defects in Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglion neurons are associated with a specific loss of TrkA-expressing neurons in the ganglion and nerves.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TrkA neurons are reduced and TrkA expression is decreased in nerves.

claim: Most TrkA neurons in Elp1 CKO at E12.5 are devoid of Elp1 protein.
source: Immunohistochemistry on E12.5 tissue sections revealed Elp1 protein expression throughout the Control trigeminal ganglion in TrkA, TrkB, and TrkC neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-C,G-I,M-O). In contrast, most TrkA neurons in Elp1 CKO were devoid of Elp1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D-F), while the majority of remaining Elp1-positive neurons expressed TrkB or TrkC (Figure 5—figure supplement 2J-L,P-R).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The majority of remaining Elp1-positive neurons in Elp1 CKO at E12.5 express TrkB or TrkC.
source: Immunohistochemistry on E12.5 tissue sections revealed Elp1 protein expression throughout the Control trigeminal ganglion in TrkA, TrkB, and TrkC neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-C,G-I,M-O). In contrast, most TrkA neurons in Elp1 CKO were devoid of Elp1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D-F), while the majority of remaining Elp1-positive neurons expressed TrkB or TrkC (Figure 5—figure supplement 2J-L,P-R).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: TrkB and TrkC neurons are born first in the trigeminal ganglion followed by TrkA neurons.
source: Consistent with reports that TrkB and TrkC neurons are born first in the trigeminal ganglion followed by TrkA neurons (Huang et al., 1999a; Huang et al., 1999b), immunohistochemistry on trigeminal ganglion serial sections revealed that all three Trk subtypes are present at E11, but the majority of established infraorbital nerve endings are either TrkB- or TrkC-positive, with little contribution from TrkA-expressing axons at this stage (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: Cited from previous studies and confirmed by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: At E11, all three Trk subtypes are present in the trigeminal ganglion, but the majority of established infraorbital nerve endings are either TrkB- or TrkC-positive, with little contribution from TrkA-expressing axons.
source: Consistent with reports that TrkB and TrkC neurons are born first in the trigeminal ganglion followed by TrkA neurons (Huang et al., 1999a; Huang et al., 1999b), immunohistochemistry on trigeminal ganglion serial sections revealed that all three Trk subtypes are present at E11, but the majority of established infraorbital nerve endings are either TrkB- or TrkC-positive, with little contribution from TrkA-expressing axons at this stage (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: By E11.5, some TrkA-positive axons have reached the whisker pad region, but the majority of infraorbital nerve endings are TrkA-negative and presumably TrkB- or TrkC-positive.
source: By E11.5, some TrkA-positive axons have reached the whisker pad region, but the majority of infraorbital nerve endings are TrkA-negative and presumably TrkB- or TrkC-positive (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: At E11.5, TrkC neurons comprise the largest proportion of neurons in the trigeminal ganglion, followed closely by TrkA, and TrkB representing the smallest proportion.
source: At this stage, TrkC neurons comprise the largest proportion of neurons, followed closely by TrkA, and TrkB representing the smallest proportion of trigeminal ganglion neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F-H, Huang et al., 1999a; Huang et al., 1999b).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and cited from previous studies.

claim: The number of TrkB and TrkC neurons does not appear to increase between E11.5 and E12.5.
source: In accordance with previous reports, the number of TrkB and TrkC neurons did not appear to increase between E11.5 and E12.5, but there was a robust increase in the number of TrkA neurons, such that TrkA neurons became the vast majority of trigeminal ganglion neurons by E12.5 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I-K; Huang et al., 1999b).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and cited from previous studies.

claim: There is a robust increase in the number of TrkA neurons between E11.5 and E12.5, such that TrkA neurons become the vast majority of trigeminal ganglion neurons by E12.5.
source: In accordance with previous reports, the number of TrkB and TrkC neurons did not appear to increase between E11.5 and E12.5, but there was a robust increase in the number of TrkA neurons, such that TrkA neurons became the vast majority of trigeminal ganglion neurons by E12.5 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I-K; Huang et al., 1999b).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and cited from previous studies.

claim: At E10.5, 88.6% of TrkA neurons, 78.0% of TrkB neurons, and 91.8% of TrkC neurons express Six1.
source: At E10.5, we observed that 88.6% of TrkA neurons, 78.0% of TrkB neurons, and 91.8% of TrkC neurons expressed Six1 (Figure 6A, D, G and J).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 6.

claim: At E11.5, 85.9% of TrkA neurons express Six1, while only 6.8% of TrkB neurons and 18.6% of TrkC neurons express Six1.
source: Surprisingly, at E11.5 and E12.5, the majority of Six1-expressing cells were TrkA neurons: 85.9% of TrkA neurons expressed Six1 at E11.5, while only 6.8% of TrkB neurons and 18.6% of TrkC neurons did (Figure 6B, E, H, and J).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 6.

claim: At E12.5, 50.6% of TrkA neurons express Six1, while only 1.8% of TrkB neurons and 6.8% of TrkC neurons express Six1.
source: Similar results were noted at E12.5, with 50.6% of TrkA neurons expressing Six1, while only 1.8% of TrkB neurons and 6.8% of TrkC neurons expressed Six1 (Figure 6C, F, I, and J).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 6.

claim: Six1 is a marker of recently differentiated neurons in the trigeminal ganglion, rather than an exclusive marker of the placodal lineage.
source: When considering the timeline of TrkA versus TrkB/TrkC neurogenesis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), these data suggest Six1 is a marker of recently differentiated neurons in the trigeminal ganglion, rather than an exclusive marker of the placodal lineage.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Six1 expression shifts from TrkB/TrkC neurons to TrkA neurons over developmental time, correlating with the timing of neurogenesis.

claim: At E10.5, 92.1% of Sox10-positive neural crest cells in the trigeminal ganglion express GFP in Wnt1-Cre; ROSAmT/mG mice.
source: In the Wnt1-Cre; ROSAmT/mG mouse, 92.1% of Sox10-positive neural crest cells in the trigeminal ganglion expressed GFP at E10.5, indicating a large proportion of neural crest cells are targeted for Wnt1-Cre-mediated recombination (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 7.

claim: At E10.5, only 12.1% of Six1-expressing cells in the trigeminal ganglion are GFP-positive in Wnt1-Cre; ROSAmT/mG mice.
source: Indeed, at E10.5, only 12.1% of Six1-expressing cells in the trigeminal ganglion were GFP-positive, confirming that the majority of Six1-positive cells are placode-derived at this stage (Figure 7E–H).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 7.

claim: At E12.5, 91.7% of Six1-positive cells in the trigeminal ganglion express GFP in Wnt1-Cre; ROSAmT/mG mice.
source: In contrast, at E12.5, 91.7% of Six1-positive cells expressed GFP, indicating a shift to mostly neural crest-derived Six1-expressing cells at later stages of trigeminal ganglion neurogenesis (Figure 7I–L).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 7.

claim: The majority of Six1-expressing cells at E10.5 are placode-derived.
source: Indeed, at E10.5, only 12.1% of Six1-expressing cells in the trigeminal ganglion were GFP-positive, confirming that the majority of Six1-positive cells are placode-derived at this stage (Figure 7E–H).
evidence: Inferred from the low percentage of Six1-positive cells that are GFP-positive (neural crest-derived) at E10.5.

claim: There is a shift to mostly neural crest-derived Six1-expressing cells at later stages of trigeminal ganglion neurogenesis (E12.5).
source: In contrast, at E12.5, 91.7% of Six1-positive cells expressed GFP, indicating a shift to mostly neural crest-derived Six1-expressing cells at later stages of trigeminal ganglion neurogenesis (Figure 7I–L).
evidence: Inferred from the high percentage of Six1-positive cells that are GFP-positive (neural crest-derived) at E12.5.

claim: At E15.5, only 24.4% of TrkA neurons express RFP (non-recombined, presumably placode-derived) in Wnt1-Cre; ROSAmT/mG mice.
source: At E15.5, only 24.4% of TrkA neurons, versus 77.4% of TrkB neurons and 78.6% of TrkC neurons, expressed RFP (Figure 8E–P).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 8.

claim: At E15.5, 77.4% of TrkB neurons and 78.6% of TrkC neurons express RFP (non-recombined, presumably placode-derived) in Wnt1-Cre; ROSAmT/mG mice.
source: At E15.5, only 24.4% of TrkA neurons, versus 77.4% of TrkB neurons and 78.6% of TrkC neurons, expressed RFP (Figure 8E–P).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and quantification shown in Figure 8.

claim: Approximately three quarters of TrkA neurons in the embryonic trigeminal ganglion are neural crest-derived.
source: These findings suggest that approximately three quarters of TrkA neurons in the embryonic trigeminal ganglion are neural crest-derived, while just one quarter of TrkB/C neurons are neural crest-derived.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that only 24.4% of TrkA neurons express RFP (placode-derived marker).

claim: Just one quarter of TrkB/C neurons in the embryonic trigeminal ganglion are neural crest-derived.
source: These findings suggest that approximately three quarters of TrkA neurons in the embryonic trigeminal ganglion are neural crest-derived, while just one quarter of TrkB/C neurons are neural crest-derived.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that approximately 77-79% of TrkB and TrkC neurons express RFP (placode-derived marker).

claim: There is a strong correlation between cellular origin and eventual Trk receptor expression in the developing trigeminal ganglion.
source: Thus, there is a strong correlation between cellular origin and eventual Trk receptor expression in the developing trigeminal ganglion, such that targeting neural crest cells will be more likely to affect TrkA versus TrkB or TrkC neurons, as seen in Elp1 CKO.
evidence: Inferred from the lineage tracing data showing that most TrkA neurons are neural crest-derived while most TrkB/TrkC neurons are placode-derived.

claim: Total TUNEL fluorescence at E12.5 is statistically higher in the Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglion compared to Control.
source: At E12.5, TUNEL fluorescent puncta were distributed throughout Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglia, and total TUNEL fluorescence was statistically higher in the E12.5 Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglion compared to Control, which only exhibited occasional, scattered TUNEL staining at this stage (Figure 9).
evidence: Demonstrated by TUNEL assay and quantification shown in Figure 9.

claim: TUNEL-positive nuclei at E12.5 are often found in TrkA-expressing cells in Elp1 CKO.
source: Indeed, TUNEL-positive nuclei were often found in TrkA-expressing cells (Figure 9G and H).
evidence: Demonstrated by TUNEL assay and immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 9.

claim: Glial precursors in the trigeminal ganglion phagocytose the cellular debris of nearby apoptotic sensory neurons.
source: This suggests that glial precursors in the trigeminal ganglion phagocytose the cellular debris of nearby apoptotic sensory neurons, as previously reported in the trunk (Wu et al., 2009).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TUNEL particles are found in glial cytoplasm but not nuclei, and cited from a previous study.

claim: Apoptosis of TrkA neurons is not explained by changes in the TrkA ligand, NGF, as NGF protein distribution in trigeminal nerve target tissues is similar between Control and Elp1 CKO.
source: Importantly, apoptosis of TrkA neurons was not explained by changes in the TrkA ligand, NGF, as NGF protein distribution in trigeminal nerve target tissues was similar between Control and Elp1 CKO (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: Aberrant TUNEL staining is not observed in Elp1 CKO geniculate ganglia compared to Control at E12.5.
source: Moreover, aberrant TUNEL staining was not observed in Elp1 CKO geniculate ganglia compared to Control at E12.5, suggesting neural crest-derived neurons are most affected by apoptosis in Elp1 CKO cranial ganglia at the examined timepoints (Figure 9—figure supplement 1E-H).
evidence: Demonstrated by TUNEL assay shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neural crest-derived neurons are most affected by apoptosis in Elp1 CKO cranial ganglia at the examined timepoints.
source: Moreover, aberrant TUNEL staining was not observed in Elp1 CKO geniculate ganglia compared to Control at E12.5, suggesting neural crest-derived neurons are most affected by apoptosis in Elp1 CKO cranial ganglia at the examined timepoints (Figure 9—figure supplement 1E-H).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that the placode-derived geniculate ganglion does not show increased apoptosis in Elp1 CKO.

claim: Deletion of Elp1 from the neural crest lineage leads to innervation defects in the head and the selective loss of TrkA neurons as a result of widespread cell death within the trigeminal ganglion.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that deletion of Elp1 from the neural crest lineage leads to innervation defects in the head and the selective loss of TrkA neurons as a result of widespread cell death within the trigeminal ganglion.
evidence: Summary inference from multiple observations including innervation defects, TrkA neuron loss, and increased apoptosis.

claim: Elp1 protein expression overlaps with β-galactosidase staining in Elp1LacZ mice, but Elp1 protein is more selectively expressed in neurons.
source: While the anatomical distribution of Elp1 protein overlapped with β-galactosidase staining in Elp1LacZ mice, the observation that Elp1 protein is more selectively expressed in neurons indicates Elp1 expression is potentially controlled at the post-transcriptional or post-translational level, such that Elp1 protein may be upregulated upon neuronal differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of Elp1 protein and β-galactosidase expression patterns.

claim: Elp1 expression may be controlled at the post-transcriptional or post-translational level, such that Elp1 protein may be upregulated upon neuronal differentiation.
source: While the anatomical distribution of Elp1 protein overlapped with β-galactosidase staining in Elp1LacZ mice, the observation that Elp1 protein is more selectively expressed in neurons indicates Elp1 expression is potentially controlled at the post-transcriptional or post-translational level, such that Elp1 protein may be upregulated upon neuronal differentiation.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed difference between Elp1 protein and β-galactosidase expression.

claim: The presence of highly enriched Elp1 protein in neuronal cytoplasm, including axonal compartments, suggests there are extranuclear functions for Elp1 in trigeminal ganglion neurons.
source: The presence of highly enriched Elp1 protein in neuronal cytoplasm, including axonal compartments, suggests there are extranuclear functions for Elp1 in trigeminal ganglion neurons, as noted in studies in other neuronal systems that localize Elp1 to axonal transport and synaptic vesicles (Abashidze et al., 2014; Naftelberg et al., 2016; Tourtellotte, 2016; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: Inferred from the subcellular localization of Elp1 protein and cited from previous studies.

claim: Elp1 is not required for trunk neural crest cell migration or subsequent formation of dorsal root or sympathetic ganglia.
source: Although migration was not directly examined here, our findings complement conclusions that Elp1 is not required for trunk neural crest cell migration or subsequent formation of dorsal root or sympathetic ganglia (Abashidze et al., 2014; George et al., 2013; Hunnicutt et al., 2012; Jackson et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from previous studies and supported by the observation that trigeminal ganglion formation appears normal at E10.5.

claim: Knockdown of Elp3 inhibits neural crest cell migration in Xenopus.
source: Interestingly, knockdown of another elongator complex member, Elp3, inhibits neural crest cell migration in Xenopus, suggesting elongator subunits may have distinct individual functions in the neural crest (Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from a previous study.

claim: Elongator subunits may have distinct individual functions in the neural crest.
source: Interestingly, knockdown of another elongator complex member, Elp3, inhibits neural crest cell migration in Xenopus, suggesting elongator subunits may have distinct individual functions in the neural crest (Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Elp1 and Elp3 have different effects on neural crest cells.

claim: At least some frontal nerve axons in Elp1 CKO are able to reach their target site but are not maintained.
source: In the ophthalmic division of Elp1 CKO, the frontal nerve initially extended branches around the eye (albeit less elaborately than in Controls, Figure 4) but then retracted by E13, resulting in an even less complex pattern of innervation (Figure 5). Therefore, at least some frontal nerve axons in Elp1 CKO are able to reach their target site but are not maintained.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that frontal nerve branches are present at E12.5 but retract by E13.

claim: Nasal nerve axons in Elp1 CKO fail to navigate to their target destinations.
source: In contrast, the medial and lateral nasal nerves (also ophthalmic division) never formed in Elp1 CKO (Figures 4 and 5), indicating nasal nerve axons failed to navigate to their target destinations.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that nasal nerves are absent in Elp1 CKO.

claim: Elp1 is required for axonal outgrowth and proper target innervation in trigeminal ganglion neurons.
source: These data suggest Elp1 is required for axonal outgrowth and proper target innervation in trigeminal ganglion neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of multiple axon outgrowth and innervation defects in Elp1 CKO.

claim: Several context-dependent mechanisms likely contribute to Elp1 CKO and FD phenotypes.
source: Even more striking is the occurrence of unique phenotypes in distinct trigeminal nerve branches upon loss of Elp1 from neural crest derivatives, indicating several context-dependent mechanisms likely contribute to Elp1 CKO and FD phenotypes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that different nerve branches show distinct phenotypes in Elp1 CKO.

claim: Reduced TrkA numbers in Elp1 CKO dorsal root ganglia have been partially attributed to early cell cycle exit and death of Pax3-positive TrkA progenitors due to reduced DNA repair.
source: A loss of TrkA neurons could potentially be explained by changes in neurogenesis or survival of TrkA-positive neurons. Reduced TrkA numbers in Elp1 CKO dorsal root ganglia have been partially attributed to early cell cycle exit and death of Pax3-positive TrkA progenitors due to reduced DNA repair (George et al., 2013; Goffena et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from previous studies.

claim: There is no difference in the number of newly differentiated (Six1-positive) neurons in E11.5 Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglia compared to Control.
source: In contrast, we observed no difference in the number of newly differentiated (Six1-positive) neurons in E11.5 Elp1 CKO trigeminal ganglia.
evidence: Stated observation from the study.

claim: Pax3-positive cells in the trigeminal ganglion express little to no Elp1 during the period of neurogenesis.
source: Moreover, Pax3-positive cells in the trigeminal ganglion express little to no Elp1 during the period of neurogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and are reportedly glial, not neuronal, progenitors (Baker et al., 2002).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and cited from a previous study.

claim: Pax3-positive cells in the trigeminal ganglion are reportedly glial, not neuronal, progenitors.
source: Moreover, Pax3-positive cells in the trigeminal ganglion express little to no Elp1 during the period of neurogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and are reportedly glial, not neuronal, progenitors (Baker et al., 2002).
evidence: Cited from a previous study.

claim: Loss of Elp1 from neural crest cells has major effects after neuronal differentiation in the trigeminal ganglion.
source: Therefore, our findings are most consistent with the idea that loss of Elp1 from neural crest cells has major effects after neuronal differentiation, but we have not definitively ruled out neurogenic deficits.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that trigeminal ganglion formation and early neurogenesis appear normal, but later defects in innervation and survival are observed.

claim: Elp1 is required for trigeminal ganglion axons to grow and properly invade target tissues in order to prevent neuronal apoptosis.
source: Collectively, our data suggest that Elp1 is required for trigeminal ganglion axons to grow and properly invade target tissues in order to prevent neuronal apoptosis.
evidence: Summary inference from multiple observations including innervation defects and increased apoptosis.

claim: Elp1 is required for the survival of TrkA neurons in sympathetic and dorsal root ganglia.
source: Our observations complement previous studies showing Elp1 is required for the survival of TrkA neurons in sympathetic and dorsal root ganglia (George et al., 2013; Jackson et al., 2014; Naftelberg et al., 2016; Li et al., 2020; Ohlen et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from previous studies.

claim: Elp1 is reported to modulate TrkA/NGF retrograde signaling by regulating the phosphorylation of TrkA receptors in signaling endosomes in sympathetic neurons.
source: In sympathetic neurons, Elp1 is reported to modulate TrkA/NGF retrograde signaling by regulating the phosphorylation of TrkA receptors in signaling endosomes (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from a previous study.

claim: The retraction of axons in the frontal nerve likely indicates an inability to receive and/or appropriately respond to target-derived neurotrophic support.
source: For those axons that successfully navigate to intended targets, deficient TrkA retrograde signaling could lead to subsequent cell death. Indeed, the retraction of axons in the frontal nerve likely indicates an inability to receive and/or appropriately respond to target-derived neurotrophic support, especially considering we and others observe no changes in the expression of NGF in Elp1 CKO target tissues (Figure 9—figure supplement 2, George et al., 2013; Morini et al., 2016; Naftelberg et al., 2016).
evidence: Inferred from the observation of axon retraction and normal NGF expression in target tissues.

claim: The loss of TrkA immunoreactivity in distal axons potentially contradicts the mechanism that Elp1 modulates TrkA retrograde signaling.
source: However, the loss of TrkA immunoreactivity in distal axons (Figure 5) potentially contradicts this mechanism since the phosphorylation state of TrkA receptors and/or retrograde transport requires adequate TrkA expression in axon terminals (Li et al., 2020; Naftelberg et al., 2016).
evidence: Inferred from the observation of reduced TrkA expression in axons and cited requirements for TrkA signaling.

claim: Some cranial nerve branches, namely the medial and lateral nasal nerves, never form in Elp1 CKO embryos, pre-empting any potential deficits in retrograde signaling.
source: Moreover, we find that some cranial nerve branches, namely the medial and lateral nasal nerves, never form in Elp1 CKO embryos, pre-empting any potential deficits in retrograde signaling.
evidence: Stated observation from the study.

claim: Neuronal Elp1 depletion can increase or decrease neurite branching in varying contexts.
source: This conclusion is further supported by contradictory observations that neuronal Elp1 depletion can increase or decrease neurite branching in varying contexts (Hunnicutt et al., 2012; Abashidze et al., 2014; Jackson et al., 2014; Ohlen et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from previous studies.

claim: Elp1 may be required for axonal outgrowth via alternative, NGF-independent mechanisms, including anterograde trafficking of receptors for critical growth factors or guidance molecules and/or regulation of local protein synthesis.
source: For example, Elp1 may be required for axonal outgrowth via alternative, NGF-independent mechanisms, including anterograde trafficking of receptors for critical growth factors or guidance molecules and/or regulation of local protein synthesis, all of which are required for growing axons (Scott-Solomon and Kuruvilla, 2018; Ascano et al., 2009; Cioni et al., 2019; Korsak et al., 2016; Batista and Hengst, 2016; Kang and Schuman, 1996).
evidence: Speculative mechanisms cited from previous studies on axon growth requirements.

claim: Elp1 has been shown to regulate neuronal gene expression in a dose-dependent manner in a humanized mouse model of FD.
source: Recently, Elp1 has been shown to regulate neuronal gene expression in a dose-dependent manner in a humanized mouse model of FD (Morini et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from a recent study.

claim: The dorsal root ganglia proteome in Elp1 CKO exhibits substantial changes across a wide range of cellular functions, including axon guidance and pathfinding.
source: Indeed, the dorsal root ganglia proteome in Elp1 CKO exhibits substantial changes (compared to Control) across a wide range of cellular functions, including axon guidance and pathfinding (Goffena et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from a previous study.

claim: Elp1 may be required for axons to respond to long-distance guidance cues.
source: In support of a potential role for Elp1 in axon pathfinding, we noted some degree of axon wandering along the ophthalmic, maxillary, and mandibular nerves in Elp1 CKO embryos (Figures 3 and 4). Perhaps in these affected neurons, Elp1 is required for axons to respond to long-distance guidance cues.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed axon wandering phenotype.

claim: Elp1 may be required for inter-axonal adhesion or to limit axonal branching in order to maintain appropriate trajectories of newly growing axons along a pre-determined tract.
source: Alternatively, Elp1 may be required for inter-axonal adhesion or to limit axonal branching in order to maintain appropriate trajectories of newly growing axons along a pre-determined tract.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed axon defasciculation phenotype.

claim: Elp1 CKO dorsal root ganglia have dramatically reduced levels of Cadherin-7.
source: Instead, we speculate the defasciculation is tied, at least in part, to defects in adhesion among axons, particularly since Elp1 CKO dorsal root ganglia have dramatically reduced levels of Cadherin-7 (Goffena et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from a previous study.

claim: In chick cranial motor neurons, Cadherin-7 enhances axonal outgrowth and restricts interstitial axon branching.
source: In chick cranial motor neurons, Cadherin-7 enhances axonal outgrowth and restricts interstitial axon branching (Barnes et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from a previous study.

claim: Elp1 plays a role in adhesion in other cell types.
source: Moreover, Elp1 plays a role in adhesion in other cell types (Johansen et al., 2008; Cohen-Kupiec et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from previous studies.

claim: In the chick trigeminal ganglion, neural crest-derived cells are reportedly found proximal to the neural tube, whereas placodal neurons are situated in distal regions.
source: In the chick trigeminal ganglion, neural crest-derived cells are reportedly found proximal to the neural tube, whereas placodal neurons are situated in distal regions (Steventon et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from a previous study.

claim: The mouse trigeminal ganglion has been previously described as a mosaic of cellular subtypes with no preferential aggregation of any particular lineage.
source: This pattern does not translate to the mouse trigeminal ganglion, which has been previously described as a mosaic of cellular subtypes with no preferential aggregation of any particular lineage (Karpinski et al., 2016; Karpinski et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited from previous studies.

claim: Anatomical position is an unreliable tool for predicting placodal versus neural crest lineage in the mouse trigeminal ganglion.
source: Therefore, anatomical position is an unreliable tool for predicting placodal versus neural crest lineage in the mouse trigeminal ganglion.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that the mouse trigeminal ganglion is a mosaic with no preferential aggregation by lineage.

claim: Studies in the chick trigeminal ganglion attribute large cell body diameter to potential placode lineage, while small diameter cells have been linked to neural crest lineage.
source: Interestingly, studies in the chick trigeminal ganglion attribute large cell body diameter to potential placode lineage, while small diameter cells have been linked to neural crest lineage (d'Amico-Martel and Noden, 1980; D'Amico-Martel and Noden, 1983).
evidence: Cited from previous studies.

claim: Murine TrkB and TrkC neurons tend to have larger cell bodies compared to small-diameter TrkA-expressing neurons.
source: Coincidently, murine TrkB and TrkC neurons tend to have larger cell bodies compared to small-diameter TrkA-expressing neurons (Fariñas et al., 1998; Huang et al., 1999a).
evidence: Cited from previous studies.

claim: Approximately two-thirds of TrkA neurons are Wnt1-Cre-recombined in the trigeminal ganglion of 8-day-old mice.
source: Our results complement a recent study which found that approximately two-thirds of TrkA neurons are Wnt1-Cre-recombined in the trigeminal ganglion of 8-day-old mice (TrkB and TrkC Wnt1-Cre ratios were not reported, Karpinski et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited from a recent study.

claim: The Trk-expressing neuronal composition within the trigeminal ganglion is established during mid- to late-gestation and remains fairly constant into early postnatal life.
source: Thus, these data indicate the Trk-expressing neuronal composition within the trigeminal ganglion is established during mid- to late-gestation and remains fairly constant into early postnatal life.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of embryonic and postnatal data.

claim: The 22q11DS deletion mouse shows targeted effects on TrkA neurons, preceded by premature neurogenic divisions of neural crest cells and increased variation of neuronal gene expression at E9.5 and E10.5.
source: Intriguingly, Karpinski et al., 2022 also reported targeted effects on TrkA neurons in the 22q11DS deletion mouse, which are preceded by premature neurogenic divisions of neural crest cells and increased variation of neuronal gene expression at E9.5 and E10.5, respectively.
evidence: Cited from a recent study.

claim: There are no observed differences in placode-derived TrkB or TrkC neurons in Elp1 CKO embryos at the examined stages.
source: In light of our conclusions, it follows that there were no observed differences in placode-derived TrkB or TrkC neurons in Elp1 CKO embryos at the examined stages.
evidence: Stated observation from the study.

claim: There are no similar neurodevelopmental perturbations in the exclusively placode-derived geniculate ganglion in Elp1 CKO at E12.5.
source: Moreover, we did not detect similar neurodevelopmental perturbations in the exclusively placode-derived geniculate ganglion, which contains few, if any, TrkA-expressing neurons at E12.5.
evidence: Stated observation from the study.

claim: Elp1 is required for the survival of TrkB-positive neurons in epibranchial ganglia.
source: Given that Elp1 is expressed in placode-derived neurons (Figure 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2), and recent reports showing Elp1 is required for the survival of TrkB-positive neurons in epibranchial ganglia (Tolman et al., 2022), we suspect a placode-targeted deletion of Elp1 would lead to TrkB neuronal deficits in the trigeminal and geniculate ganglia.
evidence: Cited from a recent study.

claim: A placode-targeted deletion of Elp1 would likely lead to TrkB neuronal deficits in the trigeminal and geniculate ganglia.
source: Given that Elp1 is expressed in placode-derived neurons (Figure 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2), and recent reports showing Elp1 is required for the survival of TrkB-positive neurons in epibranchial ganglia (Tolman et al., 2022), we suspect a placode-targeted deletion of Elp1 would lead to TrkB neuronal deficits in the trigeminal and geniculate ganglia.
evidence: Speculative prediction based on Elp1 expression in placode-derived neurons and cited studies.

claim: Placode-derived TrkB or TrkC neurons may be indirectly affected at later timepoints in Elp1 CKO, given the important reciprocal interactions between the two lineages during trigeminal ganglion development.
source: It is also possible that placode-derived TrkB or TrkC neurons will be indirectly affected at later timepoints in Elp1 CKO, given the important reciprocal interactions between the two lineages during trigeminal ganglion development (Shiau et al., 2008; Shiau and Bronner-Fraser, 2009; Wu and Taneyhill, 2019; Steventon et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: Speculative prediction based on cited studies about lineage interactions.

claim: Innervation of the whisker pad is initiated by E11.5 in both Control and Elp1 CKO.
source: For instance, innervation of the whisker pad is initiated by E11.5 in both Control and Elp1 CKO (Figure 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3.

claim: The innervation field of the whisker pad does not increase substantially in the Elp1 CKO between E11.5 and E13.
source: However, the innervation field does not increase substantially in the Elp1 CKO (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: Demonstrated by whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Placode-derived neurons may reach the whisker pad first and act as scaffolds upon which later-differentiating TrkA axons can traverse.
source: This suggests that placode-derived neurons may reach the whisker pad first and act as scaffolds upon which later-differentiating TrkA axons can traverse.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed innervation pattern.

claim: The vast majority of early maxillary nerve fibers at E11 express TrkB or TrkC, with few initial contributions of TrkA-positive axons.
source: This is supported by distinct Trk receptor expression in the maxillary nerve at E11, in which the vast majority of early maxillary nerve fibers express TrkB or TrkC, with few initial contributions of TrkA-positive axons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Wnt1-Cre driver does not target every neural crest cell.
source: An additional limitation to our studies is that the Wnt1-Cre driver does not target every neural crest cell.
evidence: Stated limitation of the study.

claim: Upward of 90% of Sox10-positive neural crest cells undergo Wnt1-Cre-mediated recombination in the trigeminal ganglion.
source: Our results are similar to previous reports in the trunk (Hari et al., 2012), in that upward of 90% of Sox10-positive neural crest cells undergo Wnt1-Cre-mediated recombination in the trigeminal ganglion (Figure 7).
evidence: Demonstrated by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 7 and cited from a previous study.

claim: A population of non-recombined neural crest derivatives is present in the trigeminal ganglion of Elp1 CKO and Wnt1-Cre; ROSAmT/mG reporter mice.
source: However, a population of non-recombined neural crest derivatives is certainly present in the trigeminal ganglion of Elp1 CKO and Wnt1-Cre; ROSAmT/mG reporter mice, which may potentially skew our analyses.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that not all neural crest cells are recombined by Wnt1-Cre.

claim: Wnt1-Cre-mediated recombination is commonly used to target neural crest cells.
source: Nonetheless, Wnt1-Cre-mediated recombination is commonly used to target neural crest cells (Debbache et al., 2018) and achieves more efficient recombination than other drivers, including Sox10-Cre (Jacques-Fricke et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from previous studies.

claim: Wnt1-Cre achieves more efficient recombination than other drivers, including Sox10-Cre.
source: Nonetheless, Wnt1-Cre-mediated recombination is commonly used to target neural crest cells (Debbache et al., 2018) and achieves more efficient recombination than other drivers, including Sox10-Cre (Jacques-Fricke et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from a previous study.

source: There are marked differences, though, in the Elp1 CKO and the presentation of FD in humans. Elp1 CKO phenotypes are more extreme due to the complete loss of Elp1 from neural crest derivatives, whereas some Elp1 protein is still present in neurons of FD patients (Slaugenhaupt et al., 2001).
evidence: Comparison of the mouse model to human disease, citing the molecular basis of FD.
